**On Maintenance**

Almost no one celebrates maintenance. We name bridges after the people who designed them, not the crews who repaint them every few years so the steel doesn't rust through. We remember the inventor of the lightbulb, not the person who changes it. And yet most of what makes the world livable isn't creation. It's upkeep.

Consider a city at 3 a.m. Someone is repairing a water main. Someone is recalibrating traffic signals, patching server software, restocking shelves, scrubbing hospital floors. None of it will make the news unless it stops happening. Maintenance is defined by its invisibility: when it's done well, nothing happens, and "nothing happening" is very hard to notice or praise.

There's a philosophical weight to this. Entropy is patient. Left alone, paint peels, gardens go wild, friendships drift, and languages lose words. Everything we value is slowly unraveling, and the only counterforce is attention, repeated endlessly, without a finish line.

I find something quietly heroic in that. The novelist who writes one brilliant book is admired, but the parent who packs lunches for eighteen years performs a different kind of devotion, one that never climaxes and never ends.

Maybe we'd live differently if we honored maintenance more. We might build things designed to be repaired rather than replaced. We might thank the people who keep the lights on. We might recognize that love, too, is mostly maintenance: not the grand declaration, but the thousandth small act of showing up.

The world isn't held together by genius. It's held together by care, practiced daily.
